title: Firouzja Demolishes Artemiev in 5-Minute Chess, Then Sets Unusual Bullet Record
summary:
GM Alireza Firouzja powered to a 6-1 lead in his Speed Chess Championship XI match against GM Vladislav Artemiev and then eased to an 11-7 victory to book a spot in the Quarterfinals against GM Javokhir Sindarov or GM Fabiano Caruana. The match set a record for the fewest 1+1 games played—just four in 25 minutes—with the 194-move first game lasting almost 10 minutes as Firouzja ran down the match clock. Artemiev's 3-1 win in that section was academic except for prize money, with Firouzja earning $6,545.14 and Artemiev $1,579.86.

The next Round of 16 match, between GMs Wesley So and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, will be on Wednesday, December 9, at 10 a.m. ET / 16:00 CET / 8:30 p.m. IST.

5+1: Firouzja 6-1 Artemiev

3+1: Firouzja 4-3 Artemiev

1+1: Firouzja 1-3 Artemiev

Firouzja joins GMs Denis Lazavik and Hikaru Nakamura in the Quarterfinals—all three players reached the live Finals of the last Speed Chess Championship and are a match away from a return to London.

2026 Speed Chess Championship Bracket

Going into the match, Firouzja was third and Artemiev ninth on the Champions Chess Tour leaderboard, which will determine 12 players who qualify for the 2027 Esports World Cup.

Champions Chess Tour Leaderboard

See full leaderboard

The Speed Chess Championship is one of three events that count toward the CCT leaderboard. The two other paths to qualification are the Titled Tuesday Grand Prix and next year's Chess.com Open. Last year's EWC champion, GM Magnus Carlsen, gets an automatic entry.

Firouzja 11-7 Artemiev

Both players have impressive records in fast chess, but the most surprising statistic going into the match is that Artemiev hasn't played in the Speed Chess Championship since 2020. Firouzja, meanwhile, is bidding to reach the final for a third time in a row.

Firouzja certainly wasn't underestimating his opponent, and told GM Aman Hambleton after the match was over: "I thought I got a very bad pairing, actually, for the first round—there were many better picks I could have had."

I thought I got a very bad pairing, actually, for the first round.

—Alireza Firouzja on facing Vladislav Artemiev

The pre-match prediction told a different story, making Firouzja a 93 percent favorite, but Hambleton and GM Eric Hansen felt that was much too high.

The prediction looked a lot more reasonable after the first section, though as Firouzja noted, "I thought 5+1 probably it would have been actually closer, but it was the reverse." Firouzja essentially won the match in 75 minutes of 5+1, with Artemiev able to claim the small consolation of outscoring his opponent in the second half.

5+1: Firouzja 6-1 Artemiev

It foretold the story of the match when Artemiev lost a hard-fought first game on time, after his position collapsed with seconds remaining.

Firouzja grabs the early lead as Artemiev loses on time in the 1st 5-minute game after his position had in any case collapsed! https://t.co/sMkPL6E88h #SpeedChess https://t.co/BaeDYNyiyu

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 27, 2026

When asked if he was focusing on the clock, Firouzja responded:

I know his style from many years—he’s always in time trouble; it’s kind of a Grischuk style. It’s not a good strategy to play on time against him because he can play very good with one second. I was always trying to play on the board, actually.

Still, in the second game Artemiev was down to five seconds against one minute and 45 seconds when he exchanged pieces on d4 and shortly afterward was hit by the crushing 28...Ra2!. There was no way back into the game.

The third game—another win for Firouzja—was much more balanced both on the clock and the board. Artemiev gave up his queen for two rooks and genuine winning chances, but Firouzja eventually won after his trapped king suddenly managed to march up the board.

Alireza Firouzja survives a tough test then marches his king to force checkmate and a 3-0 scoreline! https://t.co/pObSajYIYC #SpeedChess https://t.co/e7qXf1IP1l

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 27, 2026

That's our Game of the Day, which GM Dejan Bojkov will annotate below.

Artemiev finally got on the board with a solid draw in the next game, but it was only a brief respite, as in the next he missed a chance, got dangerously low on the clock, and ultimately got hit by the killer blow 37.Ng6!.

There's no time to take the knight as Re8+ is threatened.

The pattern continued, with Artemiev only getting a draw from a winning position in the next game, before the last of the session finished with Firouzja grinding out his fifth 5+1 win. The score was a daunting 6-1, with Hansen, referring to the largest Thanksgiving comeback in NFL history, commenting, "Artemiev just needs to treat Alireza like the Dallas Cowboys!"

Artemiev just needs to treat Alireza like the Dallas Cowboys!

—Eric Hansen

3+1: Firouzja 4-3 Artemiev

We never quite got those heroics, but after a rollercoaster draw in the first game of 3+1, Artemiev did finally grab a win when, in a very complex position, Firouzja blundered in one move.

Firouzja didn't let the loss bother him, however, and drew the next game before going on to restore a five-point lead.

Firouzja never allowed Artemiev to get close.

If one game ended the match as a contest, it was the one that followed, where, for one move after 21...e3? Artemiev could grab another win almost on the spot. Instead it was mutual blindness as he blundered in turn and went on to lose.

Instead of a four-point lead, it was a six-point lead, and two draws to end the three-minute section left that unchanged.

1+1: Firouzja 1-3 Artemiev

"You’re about to play Alireza in bullet, and that’s not a place you expect to do well in," Hambleton had noted as the 1+1 section approached, with Firouzja the Bullet Chess Champion in 2024 and 2025, and the runner-up in 2026. Firouzja himself, however, decided to leave nothing to chance. He explained afterward:

He’s a very strong bullet player, so I thought I should use all my advantage. I was six points up going to bullet, and in 25 minutes he has mathematical chances, of course—so I have to do the professional thing!

Firouzja took no chances of allowing a comeback.

The professional thing, in this case, is to use Artemiev's technical style against him and play out quiet positions for as long as humanly possible. For the first bullet game, that meant taking a position with a rook and three pawns on one side for both players and continuing until move 194!

Artemiev was partly to blame, since he'd pushed a pawn himself at one point and doomed himself to another 50 moves before he (or rather the Chess.com server) could claim a draw.

That single game had taken 10 of the 25 minutes off the match clock, and already made a comeback almost impossible. The mission was completed by the next game, where Firouzja couldn't suppress a smile as another technical position arose, though this time it ended in a modest 101 moves.

The situation was already hopeless for Artemiev, with the next game perhaps rubbing salt in the wound. Firouzja blundered a piece on move 17, but then still dragged things out until move 75, waiting over 20 seconds in the final position to lose on time instead of allowing mate-in-one.

Artemiev won again in the next game, but the fourth was already the last of the section as the match clock ran out.

A curious finish — Firouzja loses a 2nd bullet game, but he ran out the time so well that only 4 (!!) bullet games were played in 25 minutes, and he clinches the win 11-7 to reach the Quarterfinals! #SpeedChess https://t.co/BW9qPHTxO6

— Chess.com News (@ChesscomNews) November 27, 2026

The final section raised a reasonable question about whether the one-second increment should be removed from the time control. Firouzja, who recently won the Total Chess Tour Pilot that tried a shorter classical time control, said he had no objections:

I'm always in favor of shorter time controls! I will not be against it, for sure. I think it makes sense to remove the increment because we play online anyway.

I'm always in favor of shorter time controls!

—Alireza Firouzja

Firouzja is now through to play the winner of Caruana vs. Sindarov (who might by that point be the world champion) for a spot in the Semifinals in London next February. There's also serious prize money on the line in each match.

Up next in the Speed Chess Championship, however, is So vs. Praggnanandhaa. That match takes place at 10 a.m. ET / 16:00 CET / 8:30 p.m. IST on Wednesday, December 9.

How to watch?

You can watch the event on Chess.com/TV. You can also enjoy the show on our Twitch and catch all our live broadcasts on YouTube.com/Chess. Games from the event can be viewed on our events page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GMs Aman Hambleton and Eric Hansen.

The Speed Chess Championship, which starts on November 16 and culminates with Live Finals on February 7, 2027, in London, is Chess.com's most important speed chess event. Some of the biggest names in chess compete to determine the best speed chess player in the world. The games are played with time controls of 5+1, 3+1, and 1+1. The prize fund is $250,000.

title: How To Watch FIDE World Championship 2026 Game 4
summary:
The Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026 between defending World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju and Challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov resumes after the rest day with game four on Saturday, November 28, at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Gukesh will have the white pieces as the players hunt for a win after beginning with three draws. Don't miss all the action!

How to watch the Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026

You can watch the Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026 live on Chess.com/Events, Chess.com/TV and on the Chesscom Twitch and YouTube channels, while GM Hikaru Nakamura is streaming on Kick.

The live broadcast is hosted by GMs Judit Polgar and Arturs Neiksans.

The Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026 in Geneva, Switzerland decides the next world champion. Uzbek Challenger Javokhir Sindarov plays Indian Defending Champion Gukesh Dommaraju in a 14-game match, with the winner the first to 7.5 points. The players have two hours for 40 moves, then 30 minutes to the end of the game, with 30 seconds added each move from move 41 onward. The prize fund is $2,500,000, with $200,000 for a win and the remaining money split equally. If tied 7-7, a playoff will take place, starting with four games of 15+10 rapid chess.

title: Switzerland's rich chess tournament history
summary:
The 2026 World Chess Championship is taking place in Switzerland, a country with a rich chess tradition. A chess festival has been attracting amateurs and professionals for many decades, while the Alpine nation has also hosted a World Chess Championship and a Chess Olympiad. Moreover, a Candidates Tournament held there remains one of the great tournaments in chess history to this day. | Photos: Dagobert Kohlmeyer / Dutch National Archives (cover photo: 1953 Candidates Tournament in Zurich) / Maia Chiburdanidze's private archive / Biel Chess Festival

As the games between defending champion Gukesh Dommaraju and challenger Javokhir Sindarov are being played, many chess fans with an interest in history will remember highlights from past decades when Switzerland served as host for similar chess events.

Here is a non-chronological overview of major chess events held in the small Alpine country, beginning with two World Championships.

Lausanne 1998: FIDE World Championship final, Karpov v. Anand

The duel between Viswanathan Anand and Anatoly Karpov | Photo: Dagobert Kohlmeyer

At a time when the chess world was divided, Anatoly Karpov and Viswanathan Anand fought for the FIDE title in Lausanne. They had qualified for the final through a knockout tournament in Groningen. After six games (two wins each and two draws), the score stood at 3-3, and Karpov secured the title with two victories in the tiebreaks.

Reigning world champion Garry Kasparov had declined his seeded place in the semifinal because he disliked the controversial format.

Brissago 2004: World Championship final, Kramnik v. Leko

The World Championship match between Vladimir Kramnik and Peter Leko in Brissago | Photo: Dagobert Kohlmeyer

It was still unclear how exactly the split at the top of the chess world would be resolved. Yet the final between Vladimir Kramnik and Peter Leko in the small Ticino town of Brissago can be regarded as an important step towards reconciliation. Leko led before the final game, but was unable to take the title from Kramnik. Kramnik won the last game, levelled the score at 7-7 and, as defending champion, retained the world crown since the match ended drawn.

Two years later, the long-awaited reunification of the World Championship took place with the match between Kramnik and Veselin Topalov. In 2012, Kramnik played a match against Levon Aronian in Zurich, which ended in a draw.

Zurich: Candidates Tournament 1953, anniversary tournaments in 1934, 1959 and 2009

The 1953 Candidates Tournament was certainly one of the most important tournaments held on Swiss soil for many decades. The 16-player event was held to determine a challenger for world champion Mikhail Botvinnik. Vassily Smyslov won the double round-robin, in which each player had to play an astonishing 30 games, finishing ahead of David Bronstein, who had failed to take the title from the defending champion in the previous World Championship match, Paul Keres, and Samuel Reshevsky, who all finished level on points. Smyslov scored 18 points, two more than his pursuers. Bronstein's tournament book is regarded as one of the classics of chess literature.

Several strong tournaments were held in honour of the Zurich Chess Club. These marked the major anniversaries of the club, founded in 1809 and thus the oldest chess club in the world:

125 th anniversary: In 1934, Alexander Alekhine won ahead of Max Euwe and Salo Flohr. The tournament book published by the Zurich Chess Club also occupies an important place in chess literature.

150 th anniversary: In 1959, Mikhail Tal won ahead of Svetozar Gligorić and 16-year-old Bobby Fischer.

200th anniversary: Another anniversary tournament was held in 2009. In an eight-player rapid round-robin, Vladimir Kramnik finished ahead of Viswanathan Anand and Veselin Topalov.

Biel – a venue for top-level chess

At the mention of Biel, chess fans immediately think of the great chess festivals that continue to be held there to this day. But Biel's chess tradition really began in 1976 with the Interzonal tournament, as the qualifying events for the World Championship were known for many years. The choice of venue marked the 75 th anniversary of the Biel Chess Club. Bent Larsen won the tournament half a point ahead of Tigran Petrosian, Lajos Portisch and Mikhail Tal. Robert Hübner finished another half-point behind, sharing places 5 th to 7 th . Interzonal tournaments were again held in Biel in 1985 and 1993. The winners were Rafael Vaganian and Boris Gelfand.

Levon Aronian won the triathlon in 2026 | Photo: Biel Chess Festival

Master tournaments had already been held in Biel since 1968. From 1977, the year after the first Interzonal tournament, grandmaster tournaments were staged at the city in the canton of Bern. Since 2019, the grandmaster tournament has been played as a triathlon - a combination of classical chess, blitz and rapid. The tournaments have since developed into huge festivals lasting several weeks. The illustrious lists of winners read like a who's who of recent chess history and can be found on the Biel Chess Festival website .

Lucerne: Chess Olympiad 1968, 1982 and World Team Championship

In September and October 1968, Lugano hosted the 18 th Chess Olympiad. The Women's Olympiad took place a year later in Lublin. The Soviet Union won ahead of Yugoslavia and the United States, with 50 other teams taking part. Details can be found on the ChessBase Olympiad platform .

At the 1982 Chess Olympiad in Lucerne, 93 teams competed in the open section and 45 in the women's competition. At the time, this represented a new participation record. In both sections, the Soviet teams dominated, led by reigning world champions Anatoly Karpov and Maia Chiburdanidze. Details can be found on the ChessBase Olympiad platform .

Maia Chiburdanidze (left) and Tigran Petrosian (right) | Photo: Chiburdanidze private archive

Three years later, the first World Team Championship was also held in Lucerne. The next four editions of the invitational team tournament were likewise held in Lucerne: the Soviet Union won in 1985 and 1989, the United States in 1993, and Russia in 1997. In 1999, the tournament moved to Yerevan.

title: London Chess Classic - Round 3 live
summary:
While Gukesh and Sindarov are battling for the world championship title in Geneva, the 16th London Chess Classic, featuring a Masters and a Challengers section, is taking place from 25 November to 4 December. Defending champion Nodirbek Abdusattorov faces a field that includes Levon Aronian, Vasyl Ivanchuk and Nihal Sarin. The Challengers features a mix of experienced grandmasters and rising stars. Rounds kick off at 4 pm London time (5 pm CET) | Pictured: Roman Dehtiarov | Photo: London Chess Classic

Live games

Masters

Challengers

Live commentary

Since its inaugural edition in 2009, the London Chess Classic has been one of the world's most prestigious tournaments. Its list of winners includes players such as Magnus Carlsen, Viswanathan Anand, Hikaru Nakamura and Fabiano Caruana. The programme comprises the Masters and Challengers, a rapid chess tournament and several open tournaments.

The centrepiece is the Masters, a ten-player round-robin tournament which takes place from 25 November to 4 December. The top seed is 22-year-old Nodirbek Abdusattorov, who won last year's edition with 7.5 out of 9 and a performance rating of 2932.

Abdusattorov has had a successful year: he won the Tata Steel Masters in Wijk aan Zee and led the Uzbek team to gold on board one at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand in September.

Among his strongest rivals are Levon Aronian, who won the Biel Chess Festival and the Freestyle Chess Grand Slam Final in 2026, and Indian grandmaster Nihal Sarin. The field also includes chess legends such as Vasyl Ivanchuk, now 57, and Michael Adams, who won the London Chess Classic in 2023. Adams has played in every edition since 2009.

Three strong young players are also taking part: 16-year-old American Andy Woodward won the Challengers tournament in Wijk aan Zee at the beginning of 2026, 17-year-old Ukrainian Ihor Samunenkov won gold on board four at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, and Shreyas Royal became the youngest British champion of all time this year at the age of 17.

The time control is 90 minutes for 40 moves, followed by 30 minutes for the rest of the game, with a 30-second increment per move from move one.

The first two rounds will take place at venues not open to the public. From round three onwards, play will take place at the Novotel London West. The games will be broadcast online with commentary by a team of international chess experts, including Daniel King, Stuart Conquest, Keti Tsatsalashvili, David Howell and Simon Williams.

Alongside the Masters, a ten-player Challengers tournament will be held for the first time, with the winner qualifying for the 2027 Masters. The programme also includes several open tournaments. The festival will conclude on 5 and 6 December with a rapid chess tournament featuring Magnus Carlsen, Anish Giri and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave.
